modules.title: From source file to a trustworthy executable
modules.summary: Compile a tiny engineering calculation and distinguish compile, link, and runtime failures.
modules.why: A reproducible executable is the first building block of a robotics component. Being able to explain how it was built matters more than owning an elaborate editor.
explanation: A source file is a description of a program, not the running program itself. A compiler checks and translates it; a linker connects the translated pieces and required libraries. An editor may hide those steps behind a button. For this first session, make the path visible: save one file, compile it with an explicitly selected language standard, run the resulting executable, then change a number and rebuild.

Use a deliberately small engineering question: what is the total mass of three components? Write the units in variable names and in the result. Predict 1.2 + 0.8 + 0.5 = 2.5 kg on paper before compiling. The compiler can detect many language mistakes, but it cannot determine that you accidentally entered a value in grams. A successful build is evidence about the program's structure, not proof of its physical meaning.

Keep a short build note containing the compiler version, language standard, command, input, and observed output. For GCC or Clang, a starting command is g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic main.cpp -o mass. Those options are compiler-specific; an MSVC workflow uses different commands. Rebuilding a saved file should be an intentional step, because accidentally running yesterday's executable can make a correct edit appear ineffective.

example.explanation: The program prints 2.5 kg. This is a complete program; save it as main.cpp and compile with a C++ compiler.

walkthrough: Write the predicted output before running.
Compile with warnings enabled and record the complete command.
Change the final mass to 0.7, rebuild, and verify 2.7 kg.
Introduce a missing semicolon, read the first diagnostic, then repair it.
pitfalls: An IDE run button may launch an older successful build after a new build fails.
A file extension and compiler driver affect whether the source is treated as C or C++.
Adding all warning flags does not prove the absence of defects.

exercises.title: A second mass estimate
exercises.prompt: Replace the masses with the supplied values and label the output.
exercises.expected: 3.5 kg
exercises.solution: The sum is 2.4 + 0.75 + 0.35 = 3.5. Store it as double and print the unit.
exercises.extension: Add an item count to the output.

exercises.title: Separate three failure stages
exercises.prompt: Make one syntax error, one missing function definition, and one wrong arithmetic operator in separate saved versions.
exercises.inputs: A declared total() function with no definition; a missing semicolon; subtraction instead of addition
exercises.expected: A compile diagnostic, a link diagnostic, and a runnable wrong answer
hints: Change one thing at a time.
Save the first diagnostic rather than all cascaded errors.
exercises.solution: The compiler rejects syntax; the linker cannot resolve total(); the wrong operator is a logic error found by the expected result.
tests: Restore the correct source and rebuild.
Confirm the new executable timestamp changes.
exercises.extension: Write a two-sentence recovery note for each failure.

exercises.title: Rebuild from a clean folder
exercises.prompt: Copy only source and build notes into a new task folder and reproduce the result.
exercises.inputs: main.cpp and the recorded build command
exercises.expected: Same labeled 2.5 kg result
hints: Do not copy the previous executable.
Use the same compiler standard flag.
exercises.solution: A successful rebuild demonstrates that the source and notes are sufficient for this tiny project, without relying on hidden editor state.
tests: Change one mass and rebuild again.
exercises.extension: Have a future version of yourself follow the notes after a week.

exercises.title: The suspicious unchanged answer
exercises.prompt: The source says 0.7 kg but the executable still reports 2.5 kg. Diagnose without changing arithmetic again.
exercises.inputs: Last build failed because a semicolon is missing
exercises.expected: Fix the build and run the new binary; result becomes 2.7 kg
hints: Check which executable path is running.
exercises.solution: The old binary survived the failed build. Fix the first compiler error, rebuild successfully, and verify the executable location.
tests: Run from the folder named in the notes.
exercises.extension: Make your build command stop before run if compilation fails.

review.question: Does compiling prove the mass is physically correct?
review.answer: No. It checks language constraints, not units, assumptions, or source data.

review.question: Why record the compiler and standard?
review.answer: They define the build environment and help reproduce differences later.

modules.title: Types, units, and deliberate conversions
modules.summary: Use numeric types that match the question and expose assumptions in the interface.
modules.why: A rover can receive perfectly valid numbers with the wrong units. Preventing that mismatch begins with clear types and explicit conversion boundaries.
explanation: A type constrains what operations are meaningful and what values can be represented. An integer is appropriate for a count of received samples; a floating-point value is appropriate for a measured duration with fractional seconds. Neither automatically carries a physical unit. A variable named time_s is a useful first defense, while later a dedicated unit type can prevent some invalid combinations before the program runs.

Integer division discards the fractional part of its result when both operands are integers. Thus 3 / 2 yields 1, even if you subsequently store that result in a double. Write 3.0 / 2.0 or convert before the division when a fractional result is intended. Conversions should be placed where the meaning changes, such as milliseconds entering an analysis that consistently uses seconds, rather than scattered throughout the calculations.

Treat ranges and invalid values as part of the problem. A negative duration or a non-finite measurement may need rejection rather than silent correction. A cast makes a conversion explicit but does not make it sensible; narrowing a huge value into a small integer still needs a range check. During this module, stay with ordinary integer and double values, document units, and compare every formula against one hand-computable case.

example.explanation: The decimal denominator makes this floating-point division, yielding 1.5 seconds.

walkthrough: Annotate each input with its unit and plausible range.
Put conversion into one named expression or function.
Write down a rejection policy for negative and non-finite input.
pitfalls: Converting after integer division cannot restore the discarded fraction.
A cast is not an input-validation policy.
Using more decimal digits in output does not improve sensor accuracy.

exercises.title: Milliseconds at the boundary
exercises.prompt: Convert each duration to seconds without losing the fraction.
exercises.solution: Divide the millisecond value by a floating-point thousand at one documented boundary.
exercises.extension: Add a function name that states both units.

exercises.title: Rate from count and time
exercises.prompt: Compute a sample rate and reject nonpositive duration.
exercises.expected: 100 samples/s; explicit invalid-duration result
hints: Count divided by seconds gives samples/s.
exercises.solution: Use a floating-point duration and evaluate count/duration only if duration > 0.
exercises.extension: Distinguish invalid data from a valid zero rate.

exercises.title: A tiny unit wrapper
exercises.prompt: Create Seconds and Milliseconds structs and a conversion function; do not allow implicit mixed arithmetic.
exercises.expected: Seconds with value 1.25
hints: Each struct may initially contain one double.
exercises.solution: Separate types force the call site to choose the conversion explicitly, making accidental mixing more visible.
tests: Attempting an undefined mixed addition fails to compile.
exercises.extension: Add a Meters type and a speed calculation.

exercises.title: Why the rate is zero
exercises.prompt: A program calculates double dt = 20 / 1000; then divides by dt. Find the first error.
exercises.expected: dt must be 0.02 s
hints: Changing only the receiving type is insufficient.
exercises.solution: 20 / 1000 is integer division and yields zero; use 20 / 1000.0 before any rate calculation.
exercises.extension: Enable conversion warnings and explain which mistakes they do not catch.

review.question: Where should unit conversion happen?
review.answer: At a named, documented interface boundary, so internal calculations use a consistent convention.

review.question: Does double guarantee exact decimal arithmetic?
review.answer: No. Many decimal fractions are approximated; use tolerances based on the calculation.

modules.title: Functions, references, and clear contracts
modules.summary: Express a small calculation as a function with explicit inputs, outputs, and failure behavior.
modules.why: Good functions let a test exercise one engineering decision without launching a whole robot.
explanation: A function turns a useful question into an interface. Instead of a large main function that reads files, converts units, and prints a report, isolate a conversion or classification that can be called with known values. A contract states what the function accepts, what it returns, and whether it changes anything provided by the caller. Start with functions that return a value and avoid hidden global state.

Passing a small scalar by value gives the function its own copy. Passing by reference allows it to refer to an existing object; a non-const reference can modify that object. A const reference is useful for reading a larger object without copying it, but it does not extend every possible object's lifetime. References are not ownership: the referenced object must still exist for the entire use.

Make boundary policies visible. A threshold comparison should say whether equality counts, a normalization routine should specify its zero-input behavior, and an averaging function should say what happens with no samples. Naming the policy is often more valuable than making the code shorter. Draw a tiny input-output table before implementation, then turn each row into a repeatable check and retain that table when you refactor.

example.explanation: This function fragment uses a strict threshold: equality does not request review. It does not diagnose hardware safety.

walkthrough: Write the contract in plain language.
Use names that include units where useful.
Call with below, equal, and above-threshold values.
Separate the boolean decision from printing its explanation.
pitfalls: A non-const reference can hide mutation if the call site is unclear.
Returning a reference to a local variable leaves a dangling reference.
A comment and implementation can disagree at equality.

exercises.title: The exact threshold
exercises.prompt: Call needs_review with the supplied temperatures.
exercises.expected: false, false, true
exercises.solution: Only 30.1 is greater than 30.0; equality remains an ordinary observation under this stated policy.
tests: A negative temperature below the limit returns false.
Changing the limit changes the decision.
exercises.extension: Add a finite-input check.

exercises.title: Value or reference
exercises.prompt: Write scale_copy(double) returning twice its input and scale_in_place(double&) modifying it.
exercises.expected: Copy call returns 6 while x stays 3; in-place call changes x to 6
exercises.solution: Pass-by-value changes a local copy; a non-const reference refers to the caller variable.
exercises.extension: Explain which interface is easier to compose in an analysis.

exercises.title: Classify a valid measurement
exercises.prompt: Return an enum class with Invalid, Normal, and Review; reject non-finite input.
exercises.expected: Invalid, Normal, Review
exercises.solution: A dedicated invalid result avoids pretending NaN is a normal low measurement when comparisons are false.
exercises.extension: Include a reason string in a later result type.

exercises.title: Reference to a vanished result
exercises.prompt: A function declares double result locally and returns const double& referring to it. Explain and fix.
exercises.inputs: const double& twice(double x) { double result=2*x; return result; }
exercises.expected: Return double by value
hints: The local object ends at function return.
Small numeric return values do not need references.
exercises.solution: The reference dangles after return. Return the computed double value; the caller receives a valid result object.
exercises.extension: Find a similar lifetime mistake involving a local string.

review.question: Does const reference mean ownership?
review.answer: No. It restricts mutation through that reference but does not own the object.

review.question: What makes a function testable?
review.answer: Explicit inputs and outputs, a small contract, and minimal hidden dependencies.

modules.title: Vectors, arrays, strings, and valid indexes
modules.summary: Represent collections with standard containers and preserve bounds.
modules.why: Telemetry arrives in collections. Containers express ownership and size so you can focus on the meaning of the samples.
explanation: Use std::vector for an owned sequence whose size can change, std::array for a fixed-size owned collection, and std::string for ordinary owned text. These types manage their storage. This does not mean every access is automatically checked: vector operator[] assumes a valid index, while at() performs a bounds check and can throw an exception. A range-based loop avoids an index entirely when you only need each element.

Decide what an empty collection means before calculating a statistic. A sum over no values can reasonably be zero; an average requires a separate no-data result. The size of a container and its allocated capacity are different: reserving capacity does not create elements that can be indexed. This distinction becomes essential when collecting many observations efficiently without inventing data that was never received.

Pointers, iterators, and references into a vector can become invalid when it reallocates. Do not keep a reference to an element, grow the vector, and assume that reference is still usable. At this stage, finish collecting the data and then traverse it, or reacquire an element by a validated index after mutation. Clear ownership and simple traversal are better first tools than attempts to minimize every copy.

example.explanation: Each element is visited once, with no manual index. The sum is 2.5.

walkthrough: Choose fixed or variable size deliberately.
Write the empty-input policy.
Use a range loop for a sum and at() for a chosen index.
Compare size() with capacity() before and after reserve().
pitfalls: reserve(10) does not make ten elements.
An index equal to size() is already outside the collection.
Growing a vector may invalidate references into its elements.

exercises.title: Add a component
exercises.prompt: Append 0.25 to the supplied masses and sum them.
exercises.expected: 4 elements and 2.75 kg
exercises.solution: The new item changes both size and total; capacity is an implementation detail, not the count.
tests: One item equals its own sum.
exercises.extension: Print the count beside the total.

exercises.title: No measurement is different from zero
exercises.prompt: Write an average function with an explicit empty-input result.
exercises.expected: No data; 0; 4
exercises.solution: The empty vector yields nullopt; populated vectors yield sum/size. Zero is valid evidence when samples exist.
tests: A single sample is its own mean.
Mixed negative and positive samples can average zero.
exercises.extension: Document treatment of non-finite samples.

exercises.title: Select only useful samples
exercises.prompt: Copy values strictly above 25 into a new vector while retaining their original order.
hints: Do not erase while traversing for the first version.
exercises.solution: A simple range loop with if(value > 25) and push_back preserves order and avoids iterator invalidation.
exercises.extension: Implement the same behavior with a standard algorithm.

exercises.title: Reserved but nonexistent
exercises.prompt: A vector reserves capacity 5 and then writes values[0]=2. Why is that invalid?
exercises.expected: Use push_back(2) or resize(5) before valid indexing
hints: Storage and live elements are distinct.
exercises.solution: The vector still has size zero. reserve only prepares storage; push_back constructs an element and increases size.
tests: at(1) throws for the one-element vector.
exercises.extension: Explain why a lucky run does not legitimize the invalid access.

review.question: When is std::array a good choice?
review.answer: When the number of owned elements is fixed and part of the interface, such as a three-axis vector.

review.question: Why avoid keeping element references across vector growth?
review.answer: Reallocation can move storage and invalidate them.

modules.title: Structs, enums, and meaningful measurement states
modules.summary: Represent a measurement and its validity without magic numbers.
modules.why: A stale value and a valid zero require different decisions. Your data model should preserve that distinction.
explanation: A bare number loses context. A temperature sample may need a timestamp, unit convention, source identifier, and validity state. Put related values into a small struct, then give mutually exclusive states an enum class. This creates names such as Missing and Stale instead of unexplained integers. It also reduces the temptation to use an impossible-looking numeric value, such as -999, as an undocumented signal.

Keep the model as small as the problem requires. A struct with public data is reasonable for a simple record. A class with private data becomes useful when construction or mutation must preserve an invariant, such as a positive calibration scale. You do not need inheritance to organize every sensor; begin with records and ordinary functions, and add stronger boundaries where they prevent real mistakes.

Separate two questions: what was observed, and what should the application do about it? A decoder may mark a measurement Missing, while a supervisor decides whether to wait, report, or request inspection. Avoid silently carrying the previous valid value forward without keeping its original time. That practice turns absence of new evidence into apparent continuity and makes later analysis misleading.

example.explanation: The sample record groups value and context. usable does not yet check age or numeric finiteness; its contract is deliberately narrow.

walkthrough: List the states your input can genuinely have.
Build one record for each state.
Write a function handling each enum value explicitly.
Keep the timestamp associated with the original measurement.
pitfalls: An unexplained sentinel may collide with real data.
A valid status flag does not prove the numeric value is finite.
Adding inheritance before identifying invariants can obscure a simple record.

exercises.title: Three observations
exercises.prompt: Create records for valid zero, stale 12, and missing data; count usable records.
exercises.expected: Exactly one usable record
hints: Quality determines usability in this contract.
exercises.solution: Check the enum, not the numeric value. The valid zero remains a usable observation.
tests: Valid negative temperature remains usable here.
exercises.extension: Add explicit finiteness validation.

exercises.title: Age policy
exercises.prompt: Define stale as age > 2 seconds and invalid as a future timestamp.
exercises.expected: Fresh, stale, invalid
hints: Equality belongs to fresh under this policy.
exercises.solution: Compute age=now-time, reject negative age, and compare strictly with 2.
exercises.extension: Explain why both times need a common clock.

exercises.title: A calibration invariant
exercises.prompt: Design a Calibration class that cannot represent a nonpositive scale.
exercises.expected: Construction rejects zero under the stated model
hints: Keep the validation in one place.
exercises.solution: A validated constructor or factory checks finite scale > 0 before returning a usable calibration object.
tests: Negative scale rejected by this chosen model.
exercises.extension: Discuss a different instrument for which negative scale could be valid.

exercises.title: The disguised missing sample
exercises.prompt: A function checks value != -999 and ignores Quality::Missing. Repair the data contract.
exercises.expected: Not usable
hints: Numeric plausibility does not establish presence.
exercises.solution: Use the named quality state. Sentinel-only logic mistakes a copied or placeholder value for an actual observation.
tests: Valid -999 follows the explicit domain policy.
exercises.extension: Remove sentinel assumptions from the calling code.

review.question: Why use an enum class?
review.answer: It makes named states explicit and avoids many accidental implicit integer conversions.

review.question: Should a decoder decide the whole robot response?
review.answer: Usually no. Preserve evidence in the decoder and apply application policy in a separate layer.

modules.title: RAII, scope, and ownership without manual cleanup
modules.summary: Tie resources to objects and let scope handle their release.
modules.why: Long-running tools need predictable cleanup even when parsing fails or a function returns early.
explanation: Ownership answers who is responsible for releasing a resource. In modern C++, an owning object can acquire a resource during construction and release it during destruction. The object lifetime becomes the cleanup plan. std::vector owns its elements and storage; std::string owns its text; std::ifstream owns a file handle. This approach is commonly called RAII, and it removes many paths where manual cleanup could be forgotten.

A scope is a useful reasoning boundary. When a local owning object leaves scope, its destructor runs during ordinary return and normal exception unwinding. Write the resource declaration close to where it becomes necessary so the lifetime is visible. You still need to check whether acquiring or using the resource succeeded; automatic closing does not make an unreadable file readable or make output writes infallible.

Prefer values until a concrete design needs dynamic ownership. If an object truly needs one dynamic owner, std::unique_ptr expresses that relationship. std::shared_ptr represents shared ownership, which adds lifetime complexity and can form cycles. It is not a default cure for unclear design. In this module, learn to draw owner-to-resource relationships and use existing library owners before attempting a custom low-level resource wrapper.

example.explanation: The stream owns the file handle and closes it when it leaves scope. The program still distinguishes opening failure from a serious read error.

walkthrough: Draw one box for each owning object and its resource.
Add an early return and identify which owners leave scope.
Check file-open success before reading.
Use values and standard library owners before adding pointers.
pitfalls: RAII handles cleanup, not all application-level recovery.
A raw pointer alone does not document ownership.
Shared ownership can delay destruction and form cycles.

exercises.title: Early return and cleanup
exercises.prompt: Explain what happens to an ifstream when the function returns after detecting a malformed first line.
exercises.inputs: A local opened ifstream and return 3
exercises.expected: The stream destructor closes its owned handle
hints: No manual close is required for lifetime cleanup.
exercises.solution: Returning leaves the local scope, destroying the stream and releasing its file resource.
tests: Normal end of file also closes on scope exit.
exercises.extension: List a resource other than memory that benefits from RAII.

exercises.title: Single dynamic owner
exercises.prompt: Create an integer with make_unique, read it, and move ownership into a second unique_ptr.
exercises.expected: Second owner reads 42; first pointer is empty after move
hints: Check the first pointer before any later use.
exercises.solution: auto a=std::make_unique<int>(42); auto b=std::move(a); moves the owner. Dereference b, not a.
tests: a evaluates false after the move.
exercises.extension: Explain why copying unique_ptr is prohibited.

exercises.title: Avoid a resource on every branch
exercises.prompt: Refactor a function with repeated manual file-close calls into a local stream object and early error returns.
exercises.inputs: Three validation branches after opening a file
exercises.expected: Every exit path releases the handle
hints: Keep error reporting separate from cleanup.
exercises.solution: One owning stream eliminates repeated cleanup code while each branch still returns its own failure reason.
exercises.extension: Add a test that repeatedly opens and rejects files.

exercises.title: A pointer that outlives its owner
exercises.prompt: A function returns input.c_str() where input is a local std::string. Repair the interface.
exercises.inputs: const char* from local string storage
exercises.expected: Return std::string by value
exercises.solution: Return the owned string. The caller then owns a valid result rather than a pointer into destroyed storage.
tests: Use the returned string after other allocations.
Verify an empty string remains valid.
exercises.extension: Identify when a string_view would have the same lifetime problem.

review.question: What does RAII connect?
review.answer: Resource release to the lifetime of an owning object.

review.question: Why not use shared_ptr everywhere?
review.answer: It complicates ownership and lifetime, adds overhead, and can create cycles.

modules.title: Errors as part of the interface
modules.summary: Distinguish no data, invalid data, and operational failure.
modules.why: A robust component should explain why it cannot produce a result, rather than inventing a plausible value.
explanation: An error policy is a design choice that callers must understand. std::optional<T> can represent a value that is absent, but it cannot by itself explain the reason. A small result struct with a status enum and value can preserve that reason. Exceptions are another tool for propagating failures, especially where the existing library interface uses them. Avoid mixing several approaches without a clear boundary and translation policy.

Consider a mean-temperature calculation. An empty file, a malformed token, and a failed file read are different events. Returning 0 for all three destroys evidence because zero may be a valid mean. A result should let the user or calling component take the next meaningful action. This often requires a useful message with a file name or row number, without dumping irrelevant internal details.

Programmer contract violations are different from ordinary external input failures. An assertion may document an internal condition expected always to hold during development, but it is not an adequate parser for arbitrary files and may be disabled in release builds. Validate external input using normal control flow. Then test each expected failure path with as much attention as the happy path, including whether partial output has been left behind.

example.explanation: Absence is represented separately from a valid zero mean. This fragment assumes all supplied values are finite.

walkthrough: List three realistic ways your operation can fail.
Choose a result type that preserves the needed distinctions.
Write the caller's error-handling branch before the implementation.
Test empty, malformed, and unavailable input independently.
pitfalls: optional::value() on an empty optional throws; check before use or deliberately handle that exception.
Assertions must not be the only external-input validation.
Catching every exception and returning zero hides the failure.

exercises.title: Zero versus none
exercises.prompt: Evaluate mean for an empty vector and for two zeros.
exercises.expected: nullopt and 0 respectively
hints: A valid zero still has a value.
Use has_value() or the optional boolean check.
exercises.solution: An empty container has no defined arithmetic mean in this contract; two zero samples have a real mean of zero.
exercises.extension: Add finite-sample validation.

exercises.title: Useful parser result
exercises.prompt: Define statuses Ok, Empty, Malformed with a value and row number where appropriate.
exercises.inputs: Empty text; line 3 contains abc; valid numeric text
exercises.expected: Three distinguishable outcomes
hints: The row number matters for malformed input.
Do not give the success value meaning on an error.
exercises.solution: Use a struct or tagged variant whose status guides which fields a caller reads. Document the invariant explicitly.
tests: Malformed row 3 is reported as row 3.
exercises.extension: Replace the always-present value with a variant.

exercises.title: A strong output policy
exercises.prompt: A report has ten input rows and row 8 is invalid. Design an all-or-nothing output policy.
exercises.inputs: Seven accepted rows, then malformed input
exercises.expected: No final report is presented as complete
hints: A temporary output can be promoted after success.
exercises.solution: Compute into temporary state; only replace the final result after the full input passes. Keep the failure reason visible.
tests: All ten valid rows produce one complete report.
exercises.extension: Compare with an explicitly labeled partial-report policy.

exercises.title: The disappearing check
exercises.prompt: A release build no longer rejects a negative duration because the only check used assert(duration>0). Fix it.
exercises.expected: Ordinary error result in every build
hints: Input validation belongs to program behavior.
exercises.solution: Use an if branch that returns or reports InvalidDuration before division; keep an assertion only for separate internal invariants.
exercises.extension: Document which conditions are input errors and which indicate programmer defects.

review.question: What does optional omit?
review.answer: It represents absence but does not inherently explain the cause.

review.question: Should an external invalid value be handled only by assert?
review.answer: No. Use validation that remains part of the program in every build.

modules.title: Text files, parsing, and repeatable telemetry imports
modules.summary: Read small logs while preserving row numbers, units, and invalid-input evidence.
modules.why: Most early engineering software connects to files before it connects to real hardware. Reliable import is a valuable project on its own.
explanation: Treat a file format as a contract rather than a suggestion. Specify its separator, header, columns, unit conventions, blank-line behavior, and allowed number syntax. A deliberately narrow format is easier to validate than a vague imitation of every possible CSV dialect. State that your first parser supports one numeric value per line, or exactly two whitespace-separated fields, and reject anything outside that definition.

Read a complete line and then parse that line. This lets you attach a useful row number to a malformed record and detect unexpected trailing text. Formatted extraction directly from the file can leave the stream in a failed state; repeatedly trying the same operation without repairing the state or discarding the bad input can trap the program. Separate acquisition from interpretation so the parser can be tested with in-memory text.

Preserve the original data and make transformation visible. If you skip blank lines, say so; if you reject a row, record why; if you convert milliseconds to seconds, label the output accordingly. A clean summary should report how many rows were accepted and rejected. Do not silently drop inconvenient values and later claim that the remaining statistics describe the entire experiment.

example.explanation: This fragment accepts exactly two whitespace-separated numbers and assigns outputs only after that syntactic check. Add a separate finite-value and domain-validation policy.

walkthrough: Write three valid and three invalid sample lines.
Parse a string independently of file access.
Reject trailing tokens and preserve output values on failure.
Attach row numbers in the file-reading layer.
pitfalls: A simple whitespace parser is not a complete CSV parser.
Syntactic acceptance does not prove finite or physically plausible values.
while(!eof()) is not the right condition for reading records; test the read operation.

exercises.title: Two-field record
exercises.prompt: Classify each supplied line with parse_pair.
exercises.expected: Accept, reject, reject
hints: A third token is outside the contract.
exercises.solution: The first extraction must produce both fields and no remaining token may be present.
exercises.extension: Add an explicit blank-line skip policy in the caller.

exercises.title: Import accounting
exercises.prompt: Count accepted and rejected records without modifying the input file.
exercises.expected: 2 accepted, 2 rejected with row numbers 2 and 4
hints: Keep row count separate from accepted count.
exercises.solution: Increment the physical row number for each line, store valid pairs, and report invalid rows with their line number.
tests: An empty file yields zero records.
exercises.extension: Calculate a mean only from a clearly labeled accepted subset.

exercises.title: Monotonic times
exercises.prompt: Add a policy that timestamps must strictly increase after the first valid record.
exercises.expected: The third and fourth records violate the stated ordering policy
hints: Decide how a rejected row affects state.
exercises.solution: With last accepted time 1, both later times are <=1 and are rejected. Retain the original row evidence.
tests: A first negative time may be accepted if relative time is allowed.
exercises.extension: Support separate runs explicitly rather than treating resets as one run.

exercises.title: One stale value printed twice
exercises.prompt: A loop tests !input.eof(), reads into x, and prints x even after extraction fails. Repair it.
exercises.expected: Print two successful values only
hints: The read operation tells you success.
End-of-file is detected by an attempted read.
exercises.solution: Use while(input >> x) for this narrow numeric stream, or getline followed by line validation for row-level diagnostics.
tests: A trailing newline produces no duplicate.
Malformed text stops or is reported according to policy.
exercises.extension: Refactor to a line parser that continues with explicit rejection accounting.

review.question: Why parse whole lines first?
review.answer: It provides record boundaries, row-number diagnostics, and a way to reject trailing content.

review.question: What must a cleaned dataset retain?
review.answer: The transformation policy and evidence of rejected or missing records.

modules.title: Tests, debugging, and evidence of correctness
modules.summary: Use boundary cases and a debugger to explain a failure rather than merely remove its symptom.
modules.why: Autonomous software needs understandable behavior under bad input, not just a convincing demonstration.
explanation: A test translates a claim into a repeatable observation. For a function that flags values strictly above a threshold, the three essential cases are below, equal, and above. For a parser, include empty, short, malformed, and valid records. Name each test after the behavior it promises, because a future failure should communicate which contract changed rather than only which line of test code ran.

A debugger lets you stop at a chosen point and inspect actual values, call history, and control flow. First predict what should be present; then compare the program state against that prediction. When the mismatch appears, reduce the input and isolate the smallest failing function. Randomly adding print statements until the output looks acceptable can hide the underlying model error.

Compiler diagnostics and runtime tools complement tests. On supported desktop toolchains, AddressSanitizer can expose memory-access errors and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer can detect selected undefined operations on executed paths. Neither proves the whole program safe, and their availability varies by platform. Keep a normal build and a diagnostic build, document how to run both, and retain the smallest input that reproduces every bug you repair.

example.explanation: A small assertion harness illustrates three boundary cases. Assertions may be disabled by build settings, so use an explicit test runner or failure checks for a durable test suite.

walkthrough: Write the intended behavior in one sentence.
Construct the smallest boundary-case table.
Stop in the debugger immediately before the wrong decision.
Save the failing input and add a regression test before refactoring.
pitfalls: A passing test proves only the cases and properties it actually checks.
Do not count a disabled assert as an executed test.
Sanitizers detect selected runtime defects, not physical-model validity.

exercises.title: Catch equality drift
exercises.prompt: A developer changes x > limit to x >= limit. Identify the single most important regression case.
exercises.expected: The equality test fails
hints: Below and above still behave the same.
exercises.solution: The equal case distinguishes the two contracts; it must expect false for strict exceedance.
exercises.extension: Write test names that state strictness.

exercises.title: Test an average
exercises.prompt: Design a table for empty, singleton, mixed-sign, and repeated values.
exercises.expected: No data; 7; 0; 3
hints: Do not compare empty to zero.
exercises.solution: These cases check absence, the identity property for a singleton, cancellation, and a constant sequence.
tests: Check the optional has a value before reading it.
exercises.extension: Add a non-finite-input policy.

exercises.title: Minimize a failing log
exercises.prompt: A 1000-row file crashes a parser. Describe and perform a reduction process on a copied fixture.
exercises.inputs: A failure caused by one truncated final row
exercises.expected: A minimal fixture that still reproduces the same failure
hints: Remove independent sections, preserving the failure.
Do not edit the original evidence.
exercises.solution: Repeatedly remove blocks and rerun until the cause is isolated, then verify the shortened file fails for the same reason.
tests: The minimal case fails before the fix.
It passes or is cleanly rejected after the fix.
exercises.extension: Record the defect and the violated contract.

exercises.title: The test suite that never tested
exercises.prompt: A release build reports success because every check was assert and NDEBUG was defined. Repair the harness.
exercises.expected: The executable must exit nonzero on a failed check in all test configurations
hints: An if check can return failure explicitly.
exercises.solution: Use a test framework or ordinary runtime comparisons that record failures independent of assert configuration.
tests: Temporarily inject an equality bug and confirm failure.
exercises.extension: Add the test executable to CTest.

review.question: Why keep the smallest failing input?
review.answer: It makes diagnosis repeatable and becomes a focused regression test.

review.question: Can a sanitizer prove a program correct?
review.answer: No. It detects specific defects on paths that execute under its instrumentation.

modules.title: CMake, headers, libraries, and clean builds
modules.summary: Organize a calculation into a reusable library plus a test executable.
modules.why: A reusable component must build outside the one folder and editor where it was created.
explanation: Once one source file becomes inconvenient, separate the reusable logic from the executable entry point. A header declares the interface that other source files use; a source file defines non-inline functions. The compiler checks each translation unit, then the linker connects them. Keep dependencies explicit so a change in one file does not accidentally depend on an include that happened to arrive through another header.

CMake describes build targets and their relationships. A target might be a library holding telemetry calculations, an application reading files, or a test executable checking the library. Prefer target-specific configuration: language features, include directories, and linked dependencies should belong to the targets that need them. This makes the build easier to reason about than a long list of global flags.

Use an out-of-source build folder, which keeps generated build files separate from authored source. The precise compiler and generator differ across systems; the purpose is a reproducible recipe, not one universal shell command. Record configuration and build steps, then perform a clean build using only the repository contents and documented prerequisites. A successful incremental build can hide missing dependencies that a clean build reveals.

example.code:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(Telemetry LANGUAGES CXX)
add_library(telemetry telemetry.cpp)
target_compile_features(telemetry PUBLIC cxx_std_17)
add_executable(telemetry_tests tests.cpp)
target_link_libraries(telemetry_tests PRIVATE telemetry)
enable_testing()
add_test(NAME telemetry_contracts COMMAND telemetry_tests)
example.explanation: This CMakeLists.txt expects authored telemetry.cpp, its interface header, and tests.cpp. It builds a library and registers a test executable.

walkthrough: Extract one pure function into a header/source pair.
Create a library target and a separate test target.
Configure into build/, compile, and run CTest.
Repeat in a new empty build folder and compare results.
pitfalls: Putting ordinary non-inline function definitions in a widely included header can cause duplicate definitions.
A missing source file in the target can produce a linker failure.
Generated build files are not a replacement for CMakeLists.txt.

exercises.title: Know each file
exercises.prompt: Assign interface, implementation, application entry, and test responsibilities to four files.
exercises.expected: Header declares; source implements; main drives; tests verify
hints: A library need not contain main.
exercises.solution: The header is the shared contract. Both application and tests link to the same compiled implementation.
tests: Test executable has its own main.
exercises.extension: Draw the build-target dependency graph.

exercises.title: Missing implementation
exercises.prompt: A function is declared and called, but telemetry.cpp is not added to the target. Diagnose the failure.
exercises.inputs: Undefined reference/unresolved external symbol for the function
exercises.expected: Add the implementation to the library and link that library
hints: Definition is needed at link time.
exercises.solution: Confirm the signature matches, then include the source in the target and link the consuming executable against it.
tests: Removing the source recreates the failure.
exercises.extension: Explain a signature mismatch that produces a similar diagnostic.

exercises.title: One library, two clients
exercises.prompt: Build a report executable and a test executable using the same telemetry library.
exercises.expected: Both clients use the same contract and implementation
hints: Avoid copying the function into tests.
Link each target to the library.
exercises.solution: Create two executable targets with distinct entry points, each linked privately to telemetry. Test source is not the production implementation.
tests: A library change affects both clients.
Tests fail if the library result is intentionally wrong.
exercises.extension: Add a second platform build when available.

exercises.title: It only works in the old build folder
exercises.prompt: A clean build fails while a week-old build directory succeeds. Investigate before copying old outputs.
exercises.inputs: Missing generated file or undeclared dependency
exercises.expected: A documented dependency or generation step fixes clean builds
hints: Check configuration inputs and generated artifacts.
exercises.solution: Identify what the old folder supplied implicitly, then declare that dependency or build step rather than retaining accidental state.
tests: Build after changing the relevant source.
exercises.extension: Document external tool versions needed for generation.

review.question: Why create a library for the calculation?
review.answer: Both application and tests can use one implementation through an explicit interface.

review.question: What does a clean build reveal?
review.answer: Missing or undeclared dependencies that cached outputs can conceal.

modules.title: Algorithms, iterators, and measured efficiency
modules.summary: Express collection operations clearly and choose performance work using evidence.
modules.why: Telemetry analysis can grow from tens to millions of records, but readable correct code remains the baseline.
explanation: A standard algorithm communicates intent: count_if counts matching elements, sort orders them, and accumulate combines values. A hand-written loop is also appropriate when it is clearer. The goal is not to replace every loop, but to make operations recognizable and keep their boundary conditions understandable. Learn what range an algorithm receives and whether it reads, modifies, or reorders that range.

Complexity describes how work grows with input size; it is not a direct stopwatch reading. A linear scan visits each record once. Repeatedly scanning the entire history for each new record can turn a manageable task into quadratic work. Before optimizing, choose a representative dataset, record a correct reference result, and measure the operation that actually matters rather than the time to print thousands of lines.

Iteration has validity rules. Removing elements can invalidate iterators or change positions, and a comparator used for sorting must obey a consistent ordering. Avoid a comparator based on less-than-or-equal, because equality must not make both objects precede each other. For numerical data, decide how non-finite values are handled before sorting or aggregation; mysterious values should not silently enter a statistical summary.

example.explanation: The fragment counts strict threshold exceedances. Its int result assumes the count is representable; a general large-data API should retain the algorithm's count type or check conversion.

walkthrough: Write a simple loop as the reference implementation.
Implement the same operation with one standard algorithm.
Compare outputs on empty, singleton, and duplicate-containing inputs.
Measure on several input sizes without console I/O in the timed section.
pitfalls: Faster-looking syntax does not establish faster execution.
A sort comparator must not use <= as its ordering rule.
Iterator validity must be rechecked after collection mutation.

exercises.title: Count the events
exercises.prompt: Count samples strictly greater than 30 with a loop and count_if.
hints: Duplicates still count as separate samples.
exercises.solution: Both implementations should increment or count for the two 31 values only.
exercises.extension: Return the native count type rather than narrowing to int.

exercises.title: Median without losing the source
exercises.prompt: Compute a median on a copy of finite data; define an even-count rule.
exercises.expected: 4; 5 using the mean of the middle pair
hints: Empty input needs a separate result.
exercises.solution: Sorted sequences are [1,4,7] and [2,4,6,8]; choose the center or mean of the two centers.
exercises.extension: Discuss overflow-resistant averaging of large middle values.

exercises.title: Avoid repeated full scans
exercises.prompt: Maintain a running count of above-threshold samples as a stream arrives.
exercises.expected: Counts after arrivals: 0,1,2,2
hints: Update from the new record only.
Do not rescan all previous records.
exercises.solution: An increment for each new matching record makes total counting work linear in the number of arrivals.
exercises.extension: Add a fixed-window count with a documented eviction rule.

exercises.title: The broken comparator
exercises.prompt: A sort comparator returns a.value <= b.value. Explain the defect.
exercises.expected: Neither equal element should be ordered before the other by a strict less comparator
exercises.solution: Use < for ascending finite numeric values. Reject or explicitly order NaN values before relying on this simple comparator.
tests: Compare an object with itself: false.
Test duplicates and already sorted input.
exercises.extension: Write a tie-breaker by sample ID.

review.question: What does linear complexity mean?
review.answer: Work grows proportionally to the number of input elements, abstracting constant factors.

review.question: Why preserve a reference implementation?
review.answer: It provides a correctness comparison while changing algorithms or optimizing.

modules.title: Time, timestamps, and latency budgets
modules.summary: Distinguish elapsed duration, measurement age, and scheduling guarantees.
modules.why: Robotics software can use the right value too late; time is part of the data contract.
explanation: A timestamp identifies a point on a particular clock, while a duration describes a difference. std::chrono types make units explicit and reduce accidental mixing of milliseconds with seconds. For measuring local elapsed intervals, a monotonic clock such as steady_clock avoids changes caused by wall-clock adjustments. A measurement timestamp from another device still requires a documented synchronization and conversion policy before its age is meaningful.

A latency budget distributes an allowed time interval across work such as acquisition, parsing, processing, and publication. Summing nominal durations is a first model, not proof that every update meets a deadline. Operating-system scheduling, I/O waits, contention, allocation, and rare slow paths can change the observed result. Measure a distribution, include worst observed values, and state the test conditions.

Keep a distinction between educational desktop timing and validated real-time behavior. A desktop test may show that a component usually finishes in two milliseconds; it does not establish a hard upper bound on every possible execution. Begin by recording timestamps at meaningful boundaries and testing stale-data policy using a fake clock. Deterministic clock inputs make boundary tests much more reliable than tests that sleep and hope.

example.explanation: Typed durations preserve units at the interface. Negative age requires a separate clock/domain policy; this narrow function only implements the strict comparison.

walkthrough: Draw acquisition-to-result timing boundaries.
Assign units and clock domains to timestamps.
Test staleness with supplied durations instead of sleep.
Measure realistic runs and report conditions and variability.
pitfalls: Wall-clock timestamps can jump and may not be synchronized across devices.
A mean below the deadline does not establish a worst-case bound.
A type-safe duration does not validate the physical timestamp source.

exercises.title: Budget arithmetic
exercises.prompt: Sum acquisition, parsing, processing, and publication durations against a 20 ms interval.
exercises.expected: 15 ms used; 5 ms nominal remainder
hints: Do not label remainder as a guarantee.
exercises.solution: The nominal sum is 15; 20-15=5 before unmodeled variation and interference.
tests: A 20 ms sum has zero remainder.
exercises.extension: Add measured variability for each stage.

exercises.title: Stale boundary
exercises.prompt: Apply stale(age,100ms) to three ages.
exercises.expected: false,false,true
hints: Use chrono durations in the test.
exercises.solution: Equality remains fresh under this contract. A different application can choose >=, but must update the contract and tests.
exercises.extension: Add an enum result for future timestamps.

exercises.title: Fake-clock replay
exercises.prompt: Design a component that accepts now as an argument and replay an old measurement.
exercises.inputs: measurement at 1000 ms; now 1050,1100,1101; limit 100 ms
exercises.expected: Fresh,fresh,stale
hints: Keep all times on one simulated clock.
exercises.solution: Age is 50,100,101 ms. Injecting now makes the three outcomes deterministic and fast to test.
tests: Repeated replay gives the same results.
A now before measurement time is handled explicitly.
exercises.extension: Replay a sequence containing a clock reset.

exercises.title: The comforting average
exercises.prompt: A timing report lists runs [2,2,2,30] ms against a 10 ms budget and concludes the system always meets it. Correct the claim.
exercises.expected: One observed deadline miss; no hard-real-time guarantee
hints: Mean and bound answer different questions.
exercises.solution: Although the mean is 9, the 30 ms run exceeds the interval by 20. Report miss count, maximum observed duration, and test conditions.
exercises.extension: Investigate where the slow run spent time.

review.question: Why inject a clock in a test?
review.answer: It makes time-boundary cases deterministic without sleeping.

review.question: Does measured maximum equal guaranteed worst-case time?
review.answer: No. It is only the largest value observed under those test conditions.

modules.title: State machines and recoverable behavior
modules.summary: Model a simulated inspection workflow with named states, events, and transitions.
modules.why: A robot must handle missing evidence and recovery as deliberately as normal operation.
explanation: A state machine makes the current operating mode explicit. An event, together with the current state and any documented guard condition, selects a transition and possibly an action. Start on paper with a transition table. For an inspection tool, useful states could be Idle, Collecting, Review, and Complete. A timeout is an event; it should not be buried as an unrelated boolean deep inside a processing loop.

Keep transition logic separate from side effects. A pure function can return the next state and a requested action, while another layer performs logging or I/O. This separation lets you replay event sequences and verify decisions without connecting hardware. It also avoids changing the state halfway through an operation that later fails. Define what happens when an event is irrelevant or arrives twice.

Recovery is part of the model, not an exception to having a model. If a sample is missing, does the workflow pause, request another sample, or require a human review? How is the accumulated data labeled? A reset should state which evidence is retained. Use conservative simulated examples while learning; the validity of a real machine's state model depends on hazard analysis and domain requirements beyond a programming exercise.

example.explanation: This small transition function is a desktop inspection model. Unlisted events retain the current state, a policy that should be documented and tested.

walkthrough: Draw the transition table before coding.
Identify actions separately from state changes.
Replay normal, missing-input, and reset sequences.
Decide how duplicate and irrelevant events behave.
pitfalls: Several independent booleans can encode impossible combinations.
A default branch that silently accepts every unknown event may hide an integration error.
A simulated state machine is not a validated control system.

exercises.title: Normal inspection
exercises.prompt: Replay Start, GoodSample, Finish from Idle.
exercises.expected: Collecting, Collecting, Complete
hints: Follow one event at a time.
GoodSample does not change the state in this model.
exercises.solution: Start begins collection; a good sample retains it; Finish completes the workflow.
exercises.extension: Return a transition log alongside the final state.

exercises.title: Missing data path
exercises.prompt: Replay Start, MissingSample, Finish.
exercises.expected: Collecting, Review, Review
exercises.solution: The Review state does not accept Finish under the given contract; a later explicit recovery event would need a new transition.
exercises.extension: Design a reviewed-and-approved event without hiding the review.

exercises.title: Transition coverage
exercises.prompt: Create a table-driven test of all four states and all five events.
exercises.expected: 20 defined test cases
hints: Do not test only the happy path.
exercises.solution: Each row states the expected next state. Coverage of the table makes ignored-event policy visible and checks Reset everywhere.
tests: All Reset rows lead to Idle.
Only the specified Start and Finish rows change modes.
exercises.extension: Add a transition result indicating ignored versus accepted events.

exercises.title: Impossible flags
exercises.prompt: A design has is_idle=true and is_complete=true simultaneously. Refactor its representation.
exercises.expected: One enum state represents exactly one mode
hints: The flags permit combinations the model does not allow.
exercises.solution: Replace independent mode booleans with State, deriving display booleans from that single source if needed.
tests: State cannot be both Idle and Complete.
exercises.extension: Identify which other flags are independent facts and should remain separate.

review.question: Why separate transitions from I/O?
review.answer: You can test decisions deterministically and handle side-effect failure explicitly.

review.question: What should happen to an unlisted event?
review.answer: Whatever the documented policy says: reject, log, ignore, or transition; it must be deliberate.

modules.title: Queues, concurrency, and bounded work
modules.summary: Understand ownership transfer and queue overload before introducing parallel execution.
modules.why: A busy robot needs an explicit policy when input arrives faster than it can be processed.
explanation: Concurrency introduces multiple activities whose execution may overlap or interleave. Shared mutable data requires coordination; using two threads does not automatically make a task faster. Begin by separating producer and consumer responsibilities in a single-threaded simulation. Define who owns each message, when ownership transfers, and whether the consumer sees a complete immutable snapshot or a shared object that might change.

A queue absorbs temporary differences in production and consumption rates, but it cannot fix a permanent mismatch. If ten samples arrive per second and only eight are processed, backlog grows. Bound the queue and choose an explicit overload policy: reject new work, drop oldest data, keep only the latest measurement, or apply backpressure where supported. The correct choice depends on whether old samples retain value.

When threads are actually introduced, protect the whole invariant rather than only individual variables. A mutex can guard a queue plus its count; an atomic counter does not automatically make a separate container safe. Condition variables require a predicate checked under the synchronization policy. This module's exercises focus on deterministic queue behavior first, so scheduling surprises do not obscure a basic design error.

example.explanation: This single-threaded queue retains the newest capacity values. It is not thread-safe and assumes q.size() never exceeds capacity.

walkthrough: Simulate producer and consumer steps without threads.
Choose and document a finite capacity.
Record discarded or rejected messages visibly.
Only then add synchronization around every shared queue operation.
pitfalls: A bounded queue needs an overload policy, not just a number.
Protecting a size counter does not protect the container.
Thread timing should not decide whether a message is partially initialized.

exercises.title: Keep the latest three
exercises.prompt: Push 1,2,3,4,5 into an initially empty queue with capacity 3.
exercises.expected: Final queue [3,4,5]; two oldest values discarded
exercises.solution: After the fourth push drop 1; after the fifth drop 2. The remaining order is oldest-to-newest 3,4,5.
exercises.extension: Return a discard count from the queue wrapper.

exercises.title: Growing backlog
exercises.prompt: Compute backlog growth for a sustained producer and consumer mismatch.
exercises.expected: 10 unprocessed samples ignoring finite capacity
hints: Net growth is two per second.
exercises.solution: The difference is 2/s, so five seconds adds 10 records unless the policy drops or blocks work.
tests: Equal rates have no average growth.
exercises.extension: Include a finite capacity of 6 and count drops.

exercises.title: Compare overload policies
exercises.prompt: Replay the same events using drop-oldest and reject-new policies.
exercises.expected: Drop-oldest keeps [2,3,4]; reject-new keeps [1,2,3]
exercises.solution: Latest telemetry often values freshness; archival records may instead require backpressure or explicit loss handling. Document why your chosen policy fits.
exercises.extension: Add timestamps and compare final measurement ages.

exercises.title: The atomic-count illusion
exercises.prompt: A queue is modified by two threads without a lock, but its size counter is atomic. Explain why the design is still unsafe.
exercises.expected: Container access and its invariant need synchronization
hints: Atomicity belongs to that counter operation.
The deque performs other mutable operations.
exercises.solution: Guard queue operations with an appropriate mutex or use a correctly designed concurrent queue. Keep count consistent with the same invariant.
tests: Use a race detector when supported.
exercises.extension: Replace shared mutation with message ownership transfer.

review.question: Can a larger queue solve permanent overload?
review.answer: No. It increases buffering time while backlog continues to grow.

review.question: What is the first concurrency design question?
review.answer: Who owns each piece of data and which operations may access or mutate it concurrently?

modules.title: ROS 2 integration with explicit message contracts
modules.summary: Connect one tested calculation to a publisher/subscriber boundary.
modules.why: ROS 2 becomes useful when it connects understood components rather than hiding unfamiliar code behind a launch command.
explanation: A ROS 2 node is a unit of computation that communicates through interfaces such as topics, services, and actions. For a first integration, keep the engineering calculation in an ordinary tested C++ library and use a node as the adapter that receives a message, checks its meaning, calls the library, and publishes a result. This keeps framework learning from replacing ordinary software reasoning.

A message contract includes more than field types. State units, coordinate frames when relevant, timestamp meaning, validity, expected rate, and what happens when messages disappear. Matching a topic name does not guarantee matching meaning. Quality-of-service settings affect delivery behavior, and endpoints need compatible settings to communicate. Use documentation for the installed ROS distribution instead of assuming examples from another release are interchangeable.

An executor schedules callbacks; callback groups and executor choices affect concurrency. Do not assume that a callback's code is automatically isolated from every other callback or that timers imply hard-real-time deadlines. Start with one simple topic and one deterministic fixture, inspect what is actually received, and then test missing, delayed, and duplicate messages. This lesson defines the integration task; use the official installed-distribution tutorial for exact package and build commands.

example.explanation: This framework-independent adapter policy can be tested before binding it to a ROS message. It assumes timestamps share a meaningful clock and requires separate finite-value validation.

walkthrough: Complete an official publisher/subscriber tutorial for your installed distribution.
Write a message contract beside the interface definition.
Call a tested library from the callback.
Replay fresh, stale, missing, and duplicate data and record the observed policy.
pitfalls: Matching field types does not establish matching units or coordinate frames.
Incompatible QoS can prevent communication even when topic names match.
A timer callback is not by itself a hard-real-time guarantee.

exercises.title: Contract age check
exercises.prompt: Apply should_process to valid measurements with three ages.
exercises.expected: true,true,false
hints: A false validity flag overrides age.
exercises.solution: The function accepts age from zero through 0.5; older messages do not enter the calculation.
exercises.extension: Add finiteness checks.

exercises.title: Document a topic
exercises.prompt: Write a contract for a simulated temperature topic with a timestamp and quality flag.
exercises.expected: Units, clock, expected rate, validity, and missing-data policy are explicit
hints: Avoid a bare field named value.
Choose a timeout policy that is a learning assumption.
exercises.solution: A complete contract states Celsius, the simulated shared clock, nominal update rate, how quality is encoded, and how absence is reported.
tests: Consumer rejects the wrong unit convention at its adapter boundary.
Missing messages produce the documented state.
exercises.extension: Version the interface when meaning changes.

exercises.title: Replay before hardware
exercises.prompt: Feed a node a saved sequence containing valid, stale, duplicate, and absent intervals.
exercises.inputs: Sequence IDs 1,2,2,4 with a long gap before 4
exercises.expected: Logged decisions explain every accepted or rejected record
hints: A duplicate policy must be chosen.
exercises.solution: Separate freshness and duplicate checks; report the long interval as missing-data evidence rather than inventing sample 3.
tests: Replaying the fixture gives the same decisions.
exercises.extension: Compare the node output with the pure library tests.

exercises.title: Silent subscriber
exercises.prompt: A subscriber receives nothing despite matching topic names. Build a focused diagnosis.
exercises.inputs: Publisher exists; types and QoS not yet checked
exercises.expected: Verify discovery, type, QoS compatibility, and callback execution
hints: Do not immediately rewrite the calculation.
exercises.solution: Confirm both endpoints are in the intended domain, have matching message types and compatible QoS, and that the subscriber executor is running.
tests: The node logs a callback when a fixture arrives.
exercises.extension: Document the actual installed distribution and chosen QoS.

review.question: Where should reusable math live?
review.answer: In a framework-independent library with tests; the node adapts messages and policy.

review.question: What else matters besides a topic name?
review.answer: Message type, semantic contract, discovery context, QoS compatibility, and executing callbacks.

modules.title: From prototype to a reviewable engineering component
modules.summary: Package a small component with requirements, tests, limitations, and a reproducible demonstration.
modules.why: A portfolio becomes credible when another person can rebuild the result and see what it does under failure.
explanation: A useful engineering component has a bounded purpose. Write a short statement such as classify a simulated temperature record as fresh, stale, or invalid, and list what lies outside scope. Connect each requirement to at least one test or demonstration. This traceability is not bureaucracy for its own sake: it makes gaps visible when a feature changes or a new collaborator asks why the program behaves a certain way.

Preserve evidence, not only screenshots. Include source, build instructions, a small data fixture, expected outputs, tests, and a concise explanation of assumptions. Record the compiler and relevant library versions used for the demonstration. Separate measured observations from guarantees; a desktop timing plot and a successful replay are valuable, but neither certifies flight suitability or safe operation of a real mechanism.

Study mature systems after you can explain a small one. F Prime provides examples of component-oriented flight-software architecture, commands, telemetry, and testing. NASA cFS is a separate ecosystem centered on reusable flight-software services and applications. Reading them can reveal ideas to borrow, but copying a framework into a project does not transfer mission qualification. Your next step should answer one concrete learning question, not simply increase the stack.

example.explanation: This small trace table illustrates a documentation relationship. A real project may keep it in Markdown or a test-management format.

walkthrough: Choose one component with a narrow, explainable purpose.
Map requirements to tests and example outputs.
Perform a clean build and demonstration using only the README.
Write limitations and a next experiment before adding another dependency.
pitfalls: Framework adoption does not confer flight qualification.
A video without reproducible inputs is weak evidence of behavior.
A portfolio should distinguish your authored code from dependencies and generated code.

exercises.title: Requirement with a boundary
exercises.prompt: Rewrite reject old data as a testable requirement.
exercises.inputs: A chosen learning threshold of 0.5 s
exercises.expected: Reject age > 0.5 s; define equality and future timestamps
exercises.solution: A precise requirement identifies the clock assumption, strictness, output status, and test at 0.5 versus 0.5001 seconds.
exercises.extension: Record why the threshold was chosen for the simulation.

exercises.title: Evidence manifest
exercises.prompt: List the smallest files needed to reproduce a telemetry decision component.
exercises.inputs: Source, build, tests, fixture, expected result
exercises.expected: A new folder can reproduce the demonstration
hints: Do not rely on an old binary.
exercises.solution: Package authored code, CMake recipe, test executable source, input fixture, expected output, and README with assumptions and limitations.
exercises.extension: Add a machine-readable result summary.

exercises.title: Framework reading expedition
exercises.prompt: Read one F Prime tutorial and identify the equivalents of input, state, output, and test.
exercises.expected: A one-page map connecting a tutorial to your component
hints: Use framework terms only when you can define them.
exercises.solution: Map a command or port to input, component fields to state, telemetry/events to observations, and test harnesses to evidence.
tests: Every mapped element cites a source section.
Mark unknown concepts for later study.
exercises.extension: Implement one tiny tutorial only after the map makes sense.

exercises.title: Overstated portfolio claim
exercises.prompt: A README says flight-ready because it uses C++ and passes tests. Rewrite it accurately.
exercises.inputs: Desktop simulation and selected tests only
exercises.expected: A tested educational prototype with explicit coverage and limitations
exercises.solution: State the tested scenarios, platform, known gaps, and absence of operational qualification. The result can be impressive without unsupported guarantees.
tests: Limitations include untested hardware and timing assumptions.
exercises.extension: Add a risk-driven next-test list.

review.question: What makes a requirement reviewable?
review.answer: It is specific enough to connect to observable evidence and clear boundary behavior.

review.question: Why read mature frameworks later?
review.answer: You can connect their abstractions to problems you already understand instead of collecting unfamiliar machinery.

projects.title: Telemetry import workbench
projects.summary: Turn a small plain-text experiment log into a reproducible summary with honest rejection accounting.

milestones.title: Define the format
milestones.deliverable: A one-page contract and six hand-written sample records
milestones.acceptance: Columns, units, blank lines, and malformed records have explicit policies.

milestones.title: Parse independently
milestones.deliverable: A function that accepts one text line
milestones.acceptance: Valid pairs parse; missing or extra fields are rejected without altering outputs.

milestones.title: Summarize evidence
milestones.deliverable: A command-line report of accepted rows, rejected rows, and mean
milestones.acceptance: The supplied fixture gives the hand-calculated counts and mean.

milestones.title: Package the result
milestones.deliverable: Source, build notes, fixture, tests, and example output
milestones.acceptance: A clean folder reproduces the report.

testPlan: Empty file reports no data, not zero mean.
Malformed rows retain their physical line numbers.
Future or nonmonotonic timestamps follow the documented policy.
extensions: Add a separately documented CSV dialect.
Compare the report with a Python reference implementation.
portfolio: A paragraph explaining why rows were rejected.
One regression test from a real bug.
constraints: Use invented or public sample data.
Do not silently repair or overwrite original records.

projects.title: Rover inspection supervisor simulator
projects.summary: Implement and replay a state machine that can explain its response to missing inspection evidence.

milestones.title: Draw the workflow
milestones.deliverable: State/event table including invalid events
milestones.acceptance: Every state has a reset policy and every event has a defined outcome.

milestones.title: Write the transition core
milestones.deliverable: Pure next-state function
milestones.acceptance: Table-driven tests cover the full state/event product.

milestones.title: Replay scenarios
milestones.deliverable: Normal, missing-input, and recovery fixture logs
milestones.acceptance: The trace explains every accepted or ignored event.

milestones.title: Review behavior
milestones.deliverable: Short decision report and limitations
milestones.acceptance: Another reader can trace a scenario without reading all source.

testPlan: Repeated events follow a deliberate idempotency policy.
Reset behavior is tested in every state.
extensions: Add a fake clock and timeout events.
Expose the core through one ROS 2 node.
constraints: Do not connect the prototype to actuators.

projects.title: Bounded sensor-stream laboratory
projects.summary: Explore freshness, queue capacity, and processing load with deterministic simulated events.

milestones.title: Specify time
milestones.deliverable: Clock, input rate, process rate, and stale threshold
milestones.acceptance: All timestamps use the same stated simulated clock.

milestones.title: Build bounded queues
milestones.deliverable: Drop-oldest and reject-new implementations
milestones.acceptance: Both enforce capacity and count every lost record.

milestones.title: Replay overload
milestones.deliverable: A fixture with bursts and sustained overload
milestones.acceptance: Expected backlog and loss totals match hand calculations.

milestones.title: Compare policies
milestones.deliverable: Plot or table of age, loss, and completed work
milestones.acceptance: Tradeoffs are explained without claiming a universal best policy.

testPlan: Capacity zero and one work by contract.
Age equality and future timestamps are tested.
extensions: Generate a CSV for Python plots.
Introduce threads only after deterministic behavior is established.
constraints: Measured desktop timing is not a hard deadline guarantee.
Use simulated observations rather than a live safety system.

projects.title: ROS 2 environmental-data adapter
projects.summary: Connect a tested measurement classifier to a single ROS 2 communication path.

milestones.title: Keep the core portable
milestones.deliverable: Framework-independent classifier library
milestones.acceptance: Ordinary C++ tests run without starting ROS.

milestones.title: Define the message contract
milestones.deliverable: Units, timestamp convention, quality, and QoS notes
milestones.acceptance: Publisher and subscriber agree on semantics and compatible settings.

milestones.title: Integrate one path
milestones.deliverable: One publisher fixture and one processing node
milestones.acceptance: Fresh valid observations produce the expected classification.

milestones.title: Exercise failures
milestones.deliverable: Replay delayed, invalid, duplicate, and absent intervals
milestones.acceptance: Every decision is visible in logs or output status.

testPlan: Wrong or absent data cannot appear as a fresh valid zero.
Core and node agree on boundary fixtures.
Stopping the publisher exposes missing-data behavior.
extensions: Record and replay with the distribution-supported tools.
Add an integration test around the node boundary.
constraints: Use the documentation for the installed ROS distribution.
No claim of real-time or flight qualification.

projects.title: Space-component design study
projects.summary: Build a small command/state/telemetry component and compare its design with an official F Prime tutorial.

milestones.title: Bound the purpose
milestones.deliverable: Two commands and a small explicit state model
milestones.acceptance: No unbounded command surface or implicit state changes.

milestones.title: Implement a desktop component
milestones.deliverable: Commands modify state and emit structured observations
milestones.acceptance: Each command has normal and invalid-state tests.

milestones.title: Study a real framework
milestones.deliverable: Annotated map to one F Prime tutorial
milestones.acceptance: Framework-specific claims cite official documentation.

milestones.title: Publish an engineering note
milestones.deliverable: Reproducible build plus design tradeoff discussion
milestones.acceptance: The note separates implemented behavior from future integration.

testPlan: Telemetry reports the actual state after each transition.
extensions: Port the tiny component into the official tutorial workspace.
constraints: Framework use does not transfer mission assurance or qualification.

glossary.definition: A source file after preprocessing, compiled as one unit.
glossary.example: telemetry.cpp plus the headers it includes.

glossary.definition: A build tool that connects compiled definitions and libraries.
glossary.example: An unresolved function can compile at the call site yet fail at linking.

glossary.definition: Resource ownership tied to an object lifetime so destruction releases it.
glossary.example: A local ifstream closes its file when it leaves scope.

glossary.definition: An object behaves as an independent value under its documented copy and assignment operations.
glossary.example: Copying a vector produces a separate owned sequence.

glossary.definition: An alias to an existing object; it does not inherently own that object.
glossary.example: const Sample& allows reading a caller-owned record.

glossary.definition: The interval during which an object exists and can be validly used.
glossary.example: A pointer to a local string is invalid after that string is destroyed.

glossary.definition: A condition a component promises to preserve at its interface boundaries.
glossary.example: A bounded queue never contains more than its capacity.

glossary.definition: A collection change makes a previously obtained iterator unusable.
glossary.example: Vector reallocation invalidates iterators into old storage.

glossary.definition: An operation for which the language imposes no requirements on resulting program behavior.
glossary.example: Out-of-bounds vector indexing is not legitimized by one successful run.

glossary.definition: A type holding either a value or no value.
glossary.example: An empty dataset returns no mean instead of a numeric zero.

glossary.definition: Explicit input assumptions, output meaning, and failure behavior.
glossary.example: A stale check defines units, clock, and equality policy.

glossary.definition: A clock intended for elapsed-time measurement without going backward.
glossary.example: steady_clock measures a local processing interval.

glossary.definition: A mechanism that slows or stops production when downstream work cannot keep up.
glossary.example: A producer waits for queue space instead of dropping a record.

glossary.definition: Communication policies controlling delivery behavior and compatibility.
glossary.example: A ROS 2 publisher and subscriber need compatible reliability settings.

glossary.definition: A repeatable check preserving the fix for a previously observed defect.
glossary.example: A truncated final record remains in the parser test fixtures.
